residencyRequirements.description: The Marriage Act, 2014 contains no express residency requirement for divorce petitions. Petitions are in practice filed at the magistrates' court station where the parties reside ('court' means a resident magistrate's court, Marriage Act, 2014, s.2); s.67 governs recognition of foreign divorce decrees. There is no minimum duration of residency.

waitingPeriod.description: No statutory waiting period after filing. In practice the court issues a Decree Nisi made absolute after roughly 30 days to six weeks — a practice inherited from the repealed Matrimonial Causes Act; the 2014 Act itself is silent. Conciliation is voluntary/discretionary and marriage-type specific (Marriage Act, 2014, ss.64, 66(4), 68).

noFault.name: Irretrievable Breakdown of the Marriage
noFault.description: The marriage has broken down irretrievably. Under s.66(6), a marriage is deemed to have irretrievably broken down where: (a) a spouse commits adultery; (b) a spouse is cruel to the other spouse or to any child of the marriage; (c) a spouse willfully neglects the other spouse for at least two years; (d) the spouses have been separated for at least two years, whether voluntarily or by decree of the court; (e) a spouse has deserted the other spouse for at least three years; (f) a spouse has been sentenced to imprisonment for life or for a term of seven years or more; (g) a spouse suffers from incurable insanity, certified by two doctors (at least one qualified or experienced in psychiatry); or (h) any other ground the court deems appropriate.

fault.name: Adultery
fault.description: The respondent has committed one or more acts of adultery and the petitioner finds it intolerable to live with them.

fault.name: Cruelty (Physical or Mental)
fault.description: The respondent has inflicted cruelty, whether mental or physical, on the petitioner or on the children of the marriage.

fault.name: Desertion for 3+ Years
fault.description: The respondent has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of at least three years immediately preceding the date of presentation of the petition.

fault.name: Exceptional Depravity
fault.description: The respondent has exhibited exceptional depravity such that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to continue living with them.

groundsForDivorce.overarchingRequirement: There is no overarching breakdown requirement — irretrievable breakdown is itself one of the civil-marriage grounds (s.66(2)(e), particularised by s.66(6)). Grounds are marriage-type specific: s.65 (Christian), s.66 (civil), s.69 (customary), s.70 (Hindu), s.71 (Islamic law governs). NOTE: The 3-year bar on civil marriage petitions (formerly s.66(1)) was struck down by the Court of Appeal in 2022 and is no longer enforceable as of June 2025.

Voluntary/discretionary conciliation, marriage-type specific — s.64 (Christian marriages: parties may seek church reconciliation bodies), s.66(4) (civil marriages: court may refer a dispute to a conciliatory process agreed between the parties), s.68 (customary marriages: parties may undergo customary conciliation or dispute resolution). s.67 governs recognition of foreign divorce decrees.

filingFees.notes: Court filing fees vary by court and type of petition (per Kenya Gazette Notice No. 1088 of 2020). The higher end of the range applies for claims with a higher value. Pauper briefs may be filed for parties who cannot afford fees. Professional legal fees are separate and typically range from KES 70,000-500,000.

childSupportGuidelines.notes: Kenya does not have fixed child support guidelines or tables. The court considers the needs of the child, the means of both parents, and the standard of living the child was accustomed to.

spousalSupportGuidelines.notes: The court may order maintenance having regard to the means, earning capacity, needs, and obligations of each party. Maintenance may be periodic, lump sum, or secured.

threeYearBar.description: The 3-year bar on divorce petitions for civil marriages (formerly in Marriage Act, 2014, s.66(1)) was declared unconstitutional by the Court of Appeal in 2022 (National Assembly of Kenya v Kina & another, Civil Appeal 166 of 2019, [2022] KECA 548, upholding Tukero ole Kina v Attorney General [2019] eKLR). The 3-year grace period for Parliament to amend the law lapsed in June 2025 without legislative action. There is now no minimum marriage duration before filing for divorce.
threeYearBar.courtOfAppealRuling: National Assembly of Kenya v Kina & another, Civil Appeal 166 of 2019, [2022] KECA 548 (10 June 2022)

decreeProcess: In practice the court first issues a Decree Nisi (conditional decree) — a court practice inherited from the repealed Matrimonial Causes Act; the Marriage Act, 2014 itself is silent on the nisi/absolute stages. After a prescribed period (typically 30 days, to allow for reconciliation or objections), either party may apply for the Decree Absolute, which finally dissolves the marriage.
reconciliationNote: Conciliation under the Marriage Act, 2014 is voluntary and discretionary, and marriage-type specific: parties to a Christian marriage may seek reconciliation through church bodies (s.64); in civil-marriage proceedings the court may refer a dispute to a conciliatory process agreed between the parties (s.66(4)); parties to a customary marriage may undergo customary conciliation or dispute resolution (s.68). No blanket mandatory court referral applies.
mutualConsentNote: In April 2025, the High Court at Nairobi (Constitutional Petition No. E075 of 2022) confirmed that divorce by mutual consent is NOT available under Kenyan law. Petitioners must prove one of the statutory fault-based or breakdown grounds under s.66(2).
